query: In conventional alloys, loss of toughness has long been associated with grain-boundary segregation and brittle grain-boundary precipitation. By contrast, compositionally complex high-entropy alloys can suppress rapid grain coarsening and deleterious intermetallic formation and have shown favorable strength–ductility combinations and resistance to high-temperature softening and low-temperature embrittlement. These findings do not establish what governs possible toughness degradation in an initially single-phase high-entropy alloy. Under the constraint of retaining a compositionally complex alloy suitable for demanding engineering service, what testable mechanistic hypothesis explains whether and why brittle behavior emerges? Specify a controlled comparison that would distinguish the hypothesis from conventional-alloy expectations, predicted observations relative to the initial baseline, its service and loading boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and a decisive falsification outcome.

generation.hypothesis: In an initially single‐phase high‐entropy alloy (HEA), stress and moderate temperature exposure during service induce rapid, localized nanocluster formation of selected principal elements at grain boundaries. These nanoclusters reduce grain‐boundary cohesive strength, causing a transition from ductile to brittle failure that is distinct from conventional alloys.
generation.material_initial_state: A single‐phase, compositionally complex HEA (e.g., CrMnFeCoNi or a similar FCC system) without any pre‐existing grain-boundary segregation or intermetallic precipitates.
generation.intervention: Subject samples to controlled tensile deformation at intermediate service temperatures (e.g., 200–400°C) and compare to samples held at room temperature. In an additional set, introduce a microalloying element designed to suppress fast nanocluster formation at the grain boundaries.
generation.conditions: Tensile loading at intermediate temperatures relevant to service conditions, with constant strain rate; comparison with reference tests performed at room temperature where no dynamic nanosegregation is expected.
generation.structural_mediator: Stress‐induced nanoclusters (localized segregation) of principal elements (e.g., Cr, Ni, Mn) at grain boundaries.
generation.mechanism: Under service-like thermal and mechanical loading, the high entropy effect does not entirely prevent local chemical ordering. Instead, the complex interaction among multiple elements facilitates rapid and selective segregation at grain boundaries. This nanoclustering lowers the cohesive energy at the grain boundaries, undermining the capacity of dislocations to effectively blunt cracks, which leads to intergranular fracture and toughness degradation.
generation.predicted_outcome: Samples tested at intermediate temperatures will exhibit a marked increase in signs of intergranular cracking and embrittlement relative to the initial ductile state. Conversely, samples where nanocluster formation is suppressed (via microalloying) will retain higher toughness. These outcomes will be observable via microscopic (e.g., atom probe tomography, TEM) and mechanical (reduced ductility, lower impact toughness) measurements.
generation.baseline: The initial single-phase HEA exhibits balanced strength and ductility with homogeneous grain boundary chemistry and toughness under standard conditions (room temperature, low strain rate).
generation.boundary: This hypothesis applies within the service regime where the alloy is exposed to moderate temperatures and strain rates—not at extreme high temperatures where other phenomena (e.g., oxidation) dominate—and for alloys retaining the single-phase structure without deliberate second-phase precipitation.
generation.uncertainty: The precise kinetics of nanocluster formation and the critical density required for brittle transition are not fully quantified. Additionally, the role of specific elemental combinations may vary across different HEA compositions.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare multiple sets of initially single-phase HEA samples. One set is deformed at room temperature (control) while another set is tensile-deformed at intermediate temperatures (e.g., 300°C) at a constant strain rate. In a parallel experiment, add a microalloying element known to inhibit grain-boundary segregation to one set of samples. Following deformation, use atom probe tomography (APT) and high-resolution TEM to analyze the grain boundary chemistry and fracture surfaces via detailed fractography, and measure mechanical toughness (e.g., by impact or fracture toughness tests).
measurements: Grain-boundary chemical composition and detection of nanocluster formation (using APT/TEM)
Fractography analysis to identify intergranular versus transgranular fracture modes
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the intermediate-temperature deformed samples do not exhibit significant nanocluster formation at grain boundaries compared to the room-temperature controls, and if no corresponding drop in toughness or shift to intergranular fracture is observed, then the hypothesis—that dynamic nanocluster formation reduces grain-boundary cohesion leading to brittle behavior—would be falsified. Similarly, if the microalloyed samples do not show improved toughness relative to non-microalloyed samples under identical conditions, the proposed mechanism is not supported.

cited_evidence.text:
Grain boundary decohesion by nanoclustering Ni and Cr separately in CrMnFeCoNi high-entropy alloys

Abstract: Nanoclustering Cr, Ni, and Mn separately at GBs reduces GB cohesion in single-phase CrMnFeCoNi high-entropy alloys. AbstractThe loss of ductility with temperature has been widely observed in tensile tests of single-phase face-centered cubic structured high-entropy alloys (HEAs). However, the fundamental mechanism for such a ductility loss remains unknown. Here, we show that ductility loss in the CrMnFeCoNi HEA upon deformation at intermediate temperatures is correlated with cracking at grain boundaries (GBs). Nanoclustering Cr, Ni, and Mn separately at GBs, as detected by atom probe tomography, reduces GB cohesion and promotes crack initiation along GBs. We further demonstrated a GB segregation engineering strategy to avoid ductility loss by shifting the fast segregation of principal elements from GBs into preexisting Cr-rich secondary phases. We believe that GB decohesion by nanoclustering multiprincipal elements is a common phenomenon in HEAs.
